articles.text: Plans to be submitted, reviewed, approved electronically The Piedmont Planning and Public Works departments are making changes to customer counter service, effective February 28. Changes are being made in an effort to improve customer service, according to a press release issued by the City yesterday, February 15. Counter service includes unscheduled inquiries at the counter as well as by phone and email. This pilot program will be effective into the fall of 2022. The new hours will be: • Monday through Thursday: 8:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. • Closed on Friday With this pilot system, project plans will be submitted, reviewed, and approved in digital format rather than paper format. “In order to improve customer service overall while maintaining our high standard for responding to inquiries, the Planning & Building and Public Works Departments will remain open for unscheduled service during the lunch hour Monday through Thursday and devoting ourselves entirely to permit processing on Fridays. These hours are consistent with those provided by other cities in the Bay Area,” said Planning Director Kevin Jackson. articles.text: In honor of Black History Month, Mountain View Cemetery is offering a special free docent-led tour on Saturday, February 26 highlighting the lives of major African American community leaders, including Captain William Shorey, Alonzo and Jennie Prentiss, and Lydia Flood Jackson. A plethora of Black trailblazers, luminaries, and civil rights leaders are buried at Mountain View Cemetery, including Marcus Foster, the first African-American superintendent of Oakland Unified School District; Ida Louise Jackson, California’s first African-American public schoolteacher; Washington Oglesby, first Black member of the California State Bar; William Rumford, first African-American elected to statewide office. Docents Sarah Calhoun and Gia White will lead the tour and provide the rich history of these and other individuals. Participants are asked to meet at the cemetery’s main office at 5000 Piedmont Avenue at 10 a.m. on Saturday, with parking available on the main road by the Mausoleum. Face masks will be required. For more information visit: https://www.mountainviewcemetery.org/events/upcoming-events. Mountain View Cemetery.
articles.title: Mountain View Cemetery to host Black History tour on February 26

articles.text: Editor: I have never written a letter to the Piedmont Post before, but Laura Pochop’s article about shoplifting at Mulberry’s Market really made me angry. Even worse, I seem to remember a similar article she wrote in desperation a few years ago. I am disturbed there are children old enough to go alone to Mulberry’s who do not understand it is wrong to steal. (Which, by the way, is exactly the same as “forgetting to pay”.) Okay, I know, kids do stupid things, maybe it was a dare, maybe they really did forget. But it is still stealing and still wrong. Parents: this is not one of those tricky grey-area discussions like sex or drinking or marijuana where “we don’t want you to do it, but we know some kids do, and maybe you will be curious…”. Shoplifting/stealing is one of the easy discussions – don’t do it, period. It is illegal, immoral, and just plain not nice. And by the way, most times the punishment is much more severe than a “talk with Chad”. Friends: our privileged children will grow up to be leaders in their communities. We must help them learn respect for all things – shopkeepers and their merchandise included. And help them understand basic economics: “the shopkeeper first has to buy the things in the store; if someone steals it, they lose that money. If stealing happens over and over, the owner won’t have any more money and will have to close the store.” Simple. If you don’t remember, ask an old timer about the sad little store that used to be “downtown Piedmont” before Mulberry’s. Chad and Laura transformed the space and created a true community hub. We owe them our gratitude and respect. And we certainly owe them freedom from pilfering children! Please, let’s do this together. articles.text: The place of statues in public spaces is currently under great scrutiny in our society. This scrutiny includes not only statues erected to commemorate Confederate generals, soldiers and political leaders, but those erected in honor of presidents like George Washington, Thomas Jefferson, Andrew Jackson, Ulysses Grant and Theodore Roosevelt. The legitimacy of statues honoring explorers such as Christopher Columbus, Father Junipero Serra and Captain William Clark has been challenged. The Minnesota Twins have put a statue of former owner Calvin Griffith into storage. The state of Arkansas is planning on replacing its pair of statues in the rotunda of the US Capitol with those of Daisy Lee Bates and Johnny Cash. There is no lack of commentary on these happenings. Some defend the statues saying the effort to remove them is an effort to “erase history.” Others say that the time to remove memorials to oppression and oppressors, slavery and slave owners, is long past. The 45th president of the United States has bemoaned the loss of “our beautiful statues” and threatened those who attack them with jail sentences of ten years. Spor ts columnist Mark Whicker suggests “Here’s an idea; Lets quit building statues. The whole point of a statue is permanence. Unlike a plaque or a star on a sidewalk, a statue is an outsized image to preserve the person. Unfortunately, people can’t be buffed into perfection the way a statue is.” Whicker’s pragmatic assessment is in keeping with the Bible’s consistent caution when it comes to graven images, statues. Exodus 20:4 reads “You shall not make for yourself an idol, whether in the form of anything that is in heaven above, or that is on the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth.” This prohibition is aimed at keeping a barrier between the act of creating the realm of God, and the act of worshipping the realm of humans. It is concerned with the human propensity to limit and confine God to structures and representations we are comfortable with. A Golden Calf erected in the wilderness was a symbol of rebellion against YHWH and Moses, YHWH’s most prominent representative. The calf sent a message on behalf of the disgruntled populace – “Dear Holy One. We want your attention when we want it and how we want it. Anything less will result in a tantrum of epic proportions.”
articles.title: The Bible has a problem with statues

These were invitations to forget the One God’s resolute commitment to justice, care for the downtrodden and concern for the well-being of widows and orphans. Jesus acknowledged that there wasn’t much he could do to undo this act of arrogant grandiosity, but he refused to be subservient to the Emperor. His words were, “Give to Caesar that which is Caesar’s, but reserve for God that which is God’s.” In a profoundly inhumane manner, the Roman Empire erected the crucified as temporary statues. Statues to the power of the state. Statues warning against insurrection. Statues declaring who it was that deserved to be treated as human and who did not. articles.text: Health services company Curative offers COVID-19 testing in Piedmont in the Community Hall parking lot five days a week. Testing is available Monday through Friday from 8:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m. in the Community Hall parking lot at 711 Highland Avenue. The test offered is a self-collected nasal PCR test, with results available within 48 hours from receipt of the sample at the lab. There is no cost to the person being tested, and insurance is not required. PCR testing is accepted as required testing before air travel in the United States according to the Center for Disease Control. The Curative clinic will be closed on Monday, February 21, for President’s Day. At this time, appointments are not required by encouraged. More information is available at https:// cur.tv/piedmont. articles.text: Photo by Brian Mahany The Yulan Magnolia, magnolia denudata, located in the Piedmont Community Hall forecourt, is recognized in the city’s Heritage Tree program. Part 2 in a series There are so many special trees in Piedmont Park. One jewel is the Yulan Magnolia, magnolia denudata, in the center of the Piedmont Community Hall forecourt. Small children cannot resist running around and around the brick seat wall that surrounds this tree, which is also a welcome place to sit and chat in the shade. This tree was planted by arborist and former Piedmont Public Works superintendent Dave Frankel and was designated as a Heritage Tree in 2021 upon his nomination. Native to China, the Yulan magnolia is deciduous and produces a stunning display of white flowers that emerge before the leaves and marks the end of winter. It’s blooming now! This dramatic species and it’s planter are the focus of many civic and private events. Over the next few weeks, The Piedmont Post will feature a brief article and photo of a Heritage Tree. Other Heritage Trees include the large Southern magnolia at the Lexford and Hampton Triangle, nominated by Betsy Goodman, and the equally grand Southern magnolia at Hampton and Huntleigh Roads, nominated by Brian Mahany. Also included are the group of Akebono or Daybreak Cherries along the Cherry Walk in Piedmont Park near the Japanese Tea House, nominated by Nancy McHugh. The public is encouraged to seek out these trees to appreciate their beauty, history, and significance. By learning more about the trees that comprise Piedmont’s urban forest, the Park Commission hopes to inspire everyone to seek out special trees in our community and encourage nominations for 2022 Heritage Trees. Submitted nominations will be evaluated on their aesthetic, educational, or historical merits. Nominations are welcome from anyone in the community and trees must be on public property, such as parks, streets, and medians. After vetting by Public Works department arborists, qualifying trees will be forwarded to the Park Commission for review and selection. Nominations are due by March 18 and voted on at the Park Commission meeting on April 6. This year’s selections will be announced at the City Arbor Day festivities on April 28. Forms are available on the City’s website on its Heritage Tree page at https://www.piedmont. ca.gov/cms/One.aspx?portalId= 13659823&pageId=17970894 You can also view an interactive map of the existing Heritage Trees which includes photos of the trees, descriptions, locations, and names of the nominating parties. For more information, please contact Nancy Kent at nkent@piedmont.ca.gov or 510-420-3064. Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. This tree was planted by arborist and former Piedmont Public Works superintendent Dave Frankel and was designated as a Heritage Tree in 2021 upon his nomination. Native to China, the Yulan magnolia is deciduous and produces a stunning display of white flowers that emerge before the leaves and marks the end of winter. It’s blooming now! This dramatic species and it’s planter are the focus of many civic and private events. Over the next few weeks, The Piedmont Post will feature a brief article and photo of a Heritage Tree. Other Heritage Trees include the large Southern magnolia at the Lexford and Hampton Triangle, nominated by Betsy Goodman, and the equally grand Southern magnolia at Hampton and Huntleigh Roads, nominated by Brian Mahany. Also included are the group of Akebono or Daybreak Cherries along the Cherry Walk in Piedmont Park near the Japanese Tea House, nominated by Nancy McHugh. The public is encouraged to seek out these trees to appreciate their beauty, history, and significance. By learning more about the trees that comprise Piedmont’s urban forest, the Park Commission hopes to inspire everyone to seek out special trees in our community and encourage nominations for 2022 Heritage Trees. Submitted nominations will be evaluated on their aesthetic, educational, or historical merits. Nominations are welcome from anyone in the community and trees must be on public property, such as parks, streets, and medians. After vetting by Public Works department arborists, qualifying trees will be forwarded to the Park Commission for review and selection. Nominations are due by March 18 and voted on at the Park Commission meeting on April 6. This year’s selections will be announced at the City Arbor Day festivities on April 28. articles.text: Preview sale at White Elephant Sale warehouse Feb. 27 Oakland Museum of California (OMCA) is re-introducing its popular White Elephant Sale in person this year with reduced capacity. Multiple sale dates will be available in March, and the special event begins on February 27 with a preview sale. The sale, now in its 63rd year, is run exclusively by the Oakland Museum Women’s Board. The sole purpose of the board, a group of over 100 year-round members, has been to raise proceeds to support OMCA in art acquisitions, exhibitions, educational programs, capital improvements, and more. Since the Board’s inception in 1959, it has contributed over $23 million to the Museum. The White Elephant Sale, touted as Northern California’s largest rummage sale, garners a significant amount of funding for the museum. The Sale also boasts many volunteers from Piedmont – most of whom are members of the Oakland Museum Women’s Board. Last year, due to COVID-19 and the large number of participants, the sale pivoted to onlineonly for the first time. The event Oakland Museum’s White Elephant Sale returns in person. returns this year with in-person shopping experiences that comply with current safety protocols - expect to wear proper masking while shopping and to present your vaccination card. Over the five week-period of the sale, visitors may browse a range of quality, used goods. Furniture, household items, clothing, artwork, ceramics, sporting goods, music, books, and a plethora of other items will be for sale. The preview sale is on Sunday, February 27, from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. March sale dates are March 2–5, 9–12, 16–19, and 23–26. A final “blowout” sale will be held the weekend of April 2-3. Visit www.whiteelephantsale. org for donation information and to obtain tickets to the event on a date of your choosing.
articles.title: White Elephant Sale returns in person

articles.text: NOTICE OF PREPARATION OF AN ENVIRONMENTAL IMPACT REPORT City of Piedmont 2023-2031 Housing Element Update NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN that, as the Lead Agency overseeing this project’s environmental review, the City of Piedmont is soliciting comments on the scope and content of the EIR for the proposed Housing Element Update. The Housing Element is one of the seven state-mandated elements of the local General Plan and is required to be updated every eight years. The City of Piedmont is preparing the 2023- 2031 Housing Element Update to comply with the legal mandate that requires each local government to identify adequate sites for housing to meet the existing and projected housing needs for varying income-levels in the community. It is intended to provide the city with a comprehensive strategy for promoting the production of safe, decent and affordable housing, and affirmatively furthering fair housing during the housing cycle. The Housing Element Update establishes goals, policies, and actions to address the existing and projected housing needs in Piedmont. The project is applicable to the entire City of Piedmont (citywide). Additional information is available on the City’s housing policy website at: https://www.piedmontishome.org/housing-element-update Members of the public and public agencies are invited to provide comments in writing as to the scope and content of the EIR before Friday, March 18, 2022. Please mail your comments to Kevin Jackson, Planning & Building Director, City of Piedmont, 120 Vista Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611; or send via email to kjackson@piedmont.ca.gov. A Scoping Meeting will be held by the Planning Commission on March 1, 2022, at 5:30 p.m. The meeting will be held via video and teleconference. Interested parties should check the Planning Commission website for information on how to join the meeting and to confirm the meeting date, time, and agenda: https:// piedmont.ca.gov/government/commissions___committees/planning_commission

articles.text: Repair work continues on the San Carlos Avenue retaining wall project, which began on January 15. A section of the median on the 300 block of San Carlos Avenue near Oakland Avenue was leaning into the roadway on the downhill side of the landscape median. The portion of the wall being replaced is approximately 140 feet. The project was expected to take seven weeks but was delayed due to rain. Heavy rains last fall and winter disrupted work for approximately 30 days. Work was further delayed due to issues with a PG&E gas line and utility pole anchor, which had to be moved. Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales explained that the previous wall did not have rebar, and that the replacement is much stronger and will endure. “You want to do it right,” Gonzales said. “And you don’t want your kids to have to [fix it] again, or your grandkids fix it later.” City Council awarded a twophase contract to CF Contracting on August 16, 2021, with an overall construction budget of $611,000. Work on the first phase, a retaining wall on Oakland Avenue near Sunnyside Avenue, was completed late last year. Staff photos Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales (right) with City inspector Rob White, and Coastland Engineering manager Tony Fisher in front of the San Carlos Avenue retaining wall project. Daniel Gonzales discusses the San Carlos project with Tony Fisher. The length of the wall being replaced is approximately 140 feet.
articles.title: San Carlos retaining wall project

articles.text: The City of Piedmont has launched an online survey for residents to provide input on the Piedmont Community Pool programming. The pool is set to open in summer 2024; the final design phase was recently approved by City Council. The 15-minute survey is geared toward aquatic programming and focuses on the community’s interest in various programming opportunities at the new aquatic facility. The Piedmont Recreation Department compiled a wide variety of programming to start understanding the community’s interests. Guaranteed programming is listed first, followed by additional options that residents may “rank.” Guaranteed programming includes the year-round Piedmont Swim Team, high school water polo and swim teams, lap swimming, swim lessons, open swim, and lifeguard training. At the completion of the survey, an overall site plan from community workshops is available so that residents may view and provide additional comments or suggestions. The Pool Program survey is open to all ages, including youth and teens. To complete the survey, visit https://www.surveymonkey.com/r/Piedmontcommunitypoolprogramming.
articles.title: Community Pool survey still open to all residents

articles.text: In observance of Black History Month, the Rotary Club of Oakland is hosting a film screening of “Evolutionary Blues - West Oakland’s Music Legacy.” “Evolutionary Blues” is a fulllength documentary, featuring interviews with more than 30 artists who regularly played in clubs and music venues that lined the blocks of 7th Street before a charge for “urban renewal” decimated the thriving, self-sustaining Oakland Black community. It’s a story about the Great Migration, told through the lens and culture of blues musicians, many of whom never made it to national fame but were respected and acclaimed within the true blues scene. They carried the soul of their Southern roots — Alabama, Louisiana, Mississippi, Texas — to Oakland. Doors will open at 6 p.m. with the screening beginning at 7 p.m. After the screening, there will be a Q&A with the films’ Director, Cheryl Fabio. Proof of full vaccination is required. Except when eating and drinking, masks must be worn. For more information, visit https://www.oakland-rotary.org/ calendar/events/2022-02-24/ s c r e e n i n g-f i l m - e volu t io nary-blues-west-oaklands-music-legacy.
articles.title: Oakland Rotary Club hosts film screening Feb 24

articles.text: Christian Stoddard, a sophomore at Piedmont High School, recently placed first in the largest indoor archery competition in the world. Competing February 6 in the Young Adult Recurve Division in the Vegas Shoot, he gave the world a glimpse of his ultimate goal – the 2028 Olympics. Stoddard first got into the sport when he was 10 years old and rose to the top of the ranks as a 15-year-old in the Cadet division. During a family vacation to Yosemite Stoddard’s passion for archery was fueled by competition with his father, Jeff. “My dad is good at everything, he just absolutely dominated and beat everyone that day. I thought, I really want to beat him; I couldn’t let my dad win,” he said with a smile. Jeff Stoddard got all three of his sons involved in non-traditional sports at a young age, like lacrosse and hockey. Christian’s twin brother, Chase, plays competitive ice hockey with the Berkeley Bears, and his older brother Andrew was on a national championship Oakland Strokes rowing team in high school. They each chose a different sport. “It was a little bit of a sibling rivalry thing with three boys. We wanted to do something that is unique to each of us and master it,” he said. After the initial introduction, Stoddard took a class with his dad at Redwood Bowmen, an archery course near Chabot Space and Science Center, and purchased his first long bow that day. Stoddard trains for two hours a day six days a week. He shoots at an indoor range for short distance targets (16 meters) at Ohlone Archery in San Leandro, and at full length targets (60 and 70 meters) on the UC Berkeley campus on weekends. He describes archery as a battle of the mind and explained what he thinks about when shooting. “You need to have your mental thoughts in a good place, but also in the same place every shot,” Stoddard said. “In my head I see the best archer version of me; I see myself confident, strong, and fast, which helps me execute the shooting motion.” Stoddard explained. After winning the Vegas Shoot, Stoddard will head to Sacramento this weekend for the Indoor Nationals, with sights set on another first place. “I want to be in the Olympics; that is my plan,” he said Since archery is not a mainstream sport, only a handful of colleges have an archery program, namely Texas A&M and a women’s program at Cornell. With the 2028 Olympics on his mind, Stoddard plans to go to Christian Stoddard stands atop the podium with a $1,000 check after winning the Vegas Shoot Indoor Archery Competition in his age group. Upon turning 15 this year Christain Stoddard moved up a division to compete with 15-17 year olds. the Olympic Training Center in Chula Vista for athletes 18 and older once he graduates from high school. “It is not recommended to go to the Olympics while going through college,” Stoddard said. The training center is for prospective Olympic athletes of many disciplines and has a dorm setting. It offers technical school education for the first two years. For the time being, a world champion is quietly going about his business at Piedmont High, trying to balance school and competing against the top archers in the world. “It would be wonderful to get more people at school to know about it, including the teachers. It is hard to see archery as something that is more than a summer activity.” “It is not easy to convince a teacher that I need time off from homework,” Stoddard said with a smile. Christian Stoddard uses a Olympic Recurve archery bow.
articles.title: Christian Stoddard – Piedmont’s world champion in archery

articles.text: The Piedmont Community Service Crew, a teenage coed Venturing unit with the Piedmont Scout Council, is organizing an event to refurbish 5,000 N95 masks which will then be distributed to health care workers and the public who need these to better deal with the ongoing pandemic. The refurbishing task is relatively simple and can be done in large groups. The Crew has arranged with the Recreation Department to use the parking lot at the Carriage House where Dress Best for Less is located (799 Magnolia Avenue). The event will take place on Saturday, March 5, from 12:30 to 4:30 p.m., and Sunday, March 6, from 10 a.m. to 3:30 p.m. Click on https://forms.gle/vcxzRegJrpou7eqZ8 to register and come join the fun. For more information, contact Crew Advisor Ken Li at 510- 410-4283.
articles.title: Community Service Crew launches mask project

The language is grounded in the district’s mission statement and LCAP goals which reflect our shared educational values and our mutual deep concern for the intellectual and emotional wellbeing of our students.” The letter reads as follows: “Because PUSD is an exemplary school district committed to public education, which depends on a team of highly experienced and dedicated teachers who are qualified, inventive and student-oriented, APT is opening Article 16: Salary and Article 15: Benefits. “Because PUSD teachers and staff are dedicated to providing an outstanding educational experience for every student through collaboration, innovation, and professional growth, APT is opening Article 6: Hours and Professional Responsibilities. “Because PUSD and APT are dedicated to imparting knowledge and promoting creative and critical thinking in a safe, nurturing, and challenging environment in which students feel physically safe and emotionally supported as part of a caring and inclusive community, especially as we address the impacts of the pandemic, APT is opening Article 20: Class Size. articles.text: Piedmont students and teachers will be required to continue wearing masks indoors until at least February 28. The state of California’s indoor mask mandate expired February 15, and while Alameda County aligned itself with the state by dropping the mandate, the change does not apply to schools. California Secretary of Health and Human Services Dr. Mark Ghaly said on February 28 the state will make a decision on when to lift the mandate for schoolchildren. “In two weeks [February 28], confirming that the data continues to be where it is, taking time to prepare and work with the school community and the communities at large, we anticipate making the change at that point.” The state will reexamine COVID state data on case rates, positivity rates, hospitalizations, pediatric hospitalizations and vaccination rates. No numerical values were designated as thresholds for the change. On the state level, vaccination rates of elementary age students is under 33% and is of concern for Ghaly. In Piedmont 98% of its students have been vaccinated against COVID-19. In the February 9 school board meeting Supt. Randy Booker declared his intent to align with California and Alameda County Health Departments when they recommend removing masks for the indoors. “I have already informed the [school] board, that as we get more information from California Department of Public Health, and Alameda County Department of Public Health, when they look to remove those indoor masks, I will recommend that we will follow suit,” Booker said. Booker’s commitment is important since local institutions can impose their own restriction and require indoor masks if they so choose. In public comment at the board meeting, prior to Booker’s statement, a number of parents voiced their support for removing masks indoors when able. “Many of the things that make school joyful, the [things we have] memories of as adults, many decades later, have not returned,” said Piedmont parent Lindsay Thomasson, giving examples of school performances, field trips, and classroom parent volunteers. “They haven’t ever looked around the class and seen what their classmates’ and teachers’ faces look like. They don’t know what their smiles or frowns look like,” she added.
articles.title: Indoor masks at schools to remain until at least Feb. 28

articles.text: Children’s Fairyland is holding auditions for children ages 8-11 who like to sing, act and dance. Each participant is invited to prepare a three-minute audition to become an actor in Fairyland’s Children’s Theater troupe. Fill out the application first at Fairyland.formstack.com/forms/ childrens_theatre_auditions Auditions will be held in-person and should include: 1 An introduction: Kids should say their name in a loud, clear voice, and say what they will be presenting during the audition. 2 A memorized monolog, speech, poem or other text. 3 A bit of song: Songs with recorded accompaniment are great as are acapella performances. 4 Applicants can also perform a dance, play an instrument, or share any other performance skills. Following the audition, Children’s Theater representatives will speak with participants and their families in an informal interview format. No experience is necessary. Selections and casting decisions will be made by Fairyland’s artistic and education staff, based not only on stage presence and vocal quality, but also on things like enthusiasm, ability to focus, and desire to commit to the program. Since 1957, Fairyland has encouraged children to create their own live theater. The program previously called Storybook Hosts and Fairyland Personalities evolved into Children’s Theater program and has been led by Doyle Ott since 2008. In the theater program, children ages 8-11 portray characters from folk tales and Children’s literature in stage productions. They also make outside appearances representing the park at community events and parades. The deadline for applying is tomorrow, Thursday, February 17. Auditions at Children’s Fairyland auditions will take place soon.
articles.title: Deadline tomorrow for Fairyland auditions

articles.text: Deadline is March 31 Jack London State Historic Park in Glen Ellen in Sonoma County has launched its annual writing contest open to students in grades 6 through 8. The contest will be open until March 31. This year’s theme is “Building Better Communities”. The contest asks students to write a fictional story where your character(s) create and dwell in a community of their own invention that is unique, different, emerging, or overcomes something challenging. The prompt calls on young writers to be creative in describing how the community works while still telling an entertaining and engaging story. The theme of the story is a nod to famous California author Jack London’s purchase of the rural land on Sonoma Mountain. London modeled “green” farming techniques to create his vision of a cooperative community where all residents would enjoy fair working conditions and great quality of life. It was known as his “garden of good intentions.” To learn more about the basis of this theme, visit https://jacklondonpark.com/annual-young-writPhoto courtesy of Jack London Historic Park The 2021 awards ceremony at Jack London State Historic Park. From left to right: Bo Kearns (guest speaker/author & journalist), Natali Cox (1st place), Keeley Graziani (2nd place), Huntyr Ammons (honorable mention), Alina Peterson (honorable mention), not pictured – Emma Visel (3rd place). ers-contest/. Jack London State Historic Park is operated by Jack London Park Partners, the first non-profit to take up management of a state park on behalf of the people of California. Park Partners is an outgrowth group of Valley of the Moon Natural History Association, a citizens’ group established over 50 years ago to support the three parks in Sonoma County, including Jack London. Judges for the contest are volunteers. Stories are judged blindly by the panel, and cash prizes are awarded for first, second, and third place. Submissions should be in PDF format, typed, double-spaced, and no more than 2000 words. Email all questions on entry format to Kristina Ellis, at kellis@jacklondonpark.com.

The Garden’s founder, Ruth Bancroft, lived to be 109 and pioneered drought-tolerant gardening. articles.text: The smallest things can throw off a mission in space, including dust. Lunar dust in particular can cause a bunch of problems for astronauts. Apollo 17 commander Gene Cernan described it as “one of our greatest inhibitors to a nominal operation on the moon.” Unlike Earth dust, lunar dust particulates are much more abrasive, like tiny pieces of glass. On our planet, wind and water erode those sharp edges. But without wind or liquid water, lunar dust is so sharp it can wear through layers of space boots and eat away at vacuum seals of sample containers. Sounds bad, right? But wait, there’s more. Dust on the sun-facing side of the Moon is bombarded with solar radiation, giving it a positive charge that acts like static cling. Some particles become so charged they hover above the surface. And the cherry on top? It’s toxic. Lunar dust is about 50% silicon dioxide. On Earth, dusts containing silica can cause the life-threatening lung disease silicosis. All 12 people who have stepped on the Moon experienced “lunar hay fever” from dust tracked into the lunar lander. Plus, with less gravity on the Moon, anything that moves around is going to kick up buckets of loose, ultra-fine, ultrasharp, clinging toxic powder. That’s why it’s crucial to understand how to handle this headache. One dusty endeavor was NASA’s Lunar Atmosphere and Dust Environment Explorer – LADEE. Designed, built, and tested at the NASA Ames Research Center, LADEE recorded impacts from more than 11,000 particles while it passed through a dust cloud engulfing the Moon. As NASA prepares to return to the Moon and then onward to Mars, data collected by LADEE and experiments done in Ames’ Lunar Regolith Test bed will be essential for preventing lunar hay fever and protecting precious equipment. You can see a full-scale frame model of LADEE currently on display at the Chabot Space & Science Center in our new NASA Ames Visitor Center. Chabot Space & Science Center is a non-profit institution, community resource, and hub for interactive STEAM engagement at 10000 Skyline Boulevard in the Oakland hills. Founded in 1883, Chabot’s mission is to inspire and educate learners of all ages about the universe and planet Earth.
articles.title: Moon dust is way worse than you think

That’s why it’s crucial to understand how to handle this headache. One dusty endeavor was NASA’s Lunar Atmosphere and Dust Environment Explorer – LADEE. Designed, built, and tested at the NASA Ames Research Center, LADEE recorded impacts from more than 11,000 particles while it passed through a dust cloud engulfing the Moon. As NASA prepares to return to the Moon and then onward to Mars, data collected by LADEE and experiments done in Ames’ Lunar Regolith Test bed will be essential for preventing lunar hay fever and protecting precious equipment. You can see a full-scale frame model of LADEE currently on display at the Chabot Space & Science Center in our new NASA Ames Visitor Center. Chabot Space & Science Center is a non-profit institution, community resource, and hub for interactive STEAM engagement at 10000 Skyline Boulevard in the Oakland hills. Founded in 1883, Chabot’s mission is to inspire and educate learners of all ages about the universe and planet Earth. The Garden’s founder, Ruth Bancroft, lived to be 109 and pioneered drought-tolerant gardening. Open to the public year-round, the Garden showcases fabulous blooms during every season and highlights plant structure and texture in robust plantings. Remember the Red Baron and other wooden sculptures sticking out of the Emeryville Bay Mudflats visible from I-80? The sculptures may have sunk into the bay, but there’s a hike around Albany point with many similar driftwood or metal sculptures still intact. Hop along the trails, stones and shorelines in a truly unique environment. Head to the Bay with the kids, the dog and a camera for the artwalk. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. The Post will publish the weekly street sweeping schedule from now through February, 2022. articles.text: On January 22-23, Scouts from Troop 15 camped at Pinnacles National Park, near Soledad in Salinas County. After a 2 ½ hour trip in a car caravan from Piedmont, 46 scouts and 13 adults set up their tent village on the valley floor 900 feet below the peaks. With sack lunches and water in day packs, the Scouts set off on a five-mile hike that included 1,400 feet of elevation gain. The steep climb to the summit followed steps carved in the rocks in some places. The Scouts enjoyed lunch atop large boulders offering stunning views of the surrounding peaks. While having lunch, they witnessed two enormous condors flying above them. “We felt so fortunate to watch two very rare California Condors soaring overhead,” said Scoutmaster Glen Tripp. The Scouts descended to Bear Gulch Reservoir to regroup and prepare their headlamps before entering some caves. The caves were formed over the eons as large boulders from the pinnacles above were shaken loose by Zachary Barber ascends the steep face safely by holding the railing. Christiane Zuber and Morgan Bishop climb the steep steps cut into the rock. Photos by Becky Spies This cluster of ancient volcanic up-flows forms a ‘pinnacle’ and is one of several such clusters in a row at Pinnacles National Park. Scouts (below in distance) are dwarfed by the geologic formations. Gabriel Barbosa, Jonah Kim, Alex Chin, Daniel Lou, Scoutmaster Glen Tripp, Tenzing Helgesen and Sammy Ragones enjoyed good conditions for a rigorous hike. A railing keeps Scout Aidan Weiss safe while studying volcanic rock while hiking. earthquakes. “The boulders were as big as two-story cabins,” noted Scout Nate Woodley. Waterfalls cascaded in the crevasse, creating a stream next to the rocky path. The Bear Gulch Caves are home to 14 species of bats. After leaving the Talus caves, the Troop hiked to its campsite to prepare dinner. Each patrol of about eight Scouts worked together to cook their meal in the hour before sundown. For some, it was their first time cooking away from their homes. Many patrols cooked classic burgers and some made fruit cobblers in Dutch ovens for dessert. “Our Scouts are really taking their cooking to the next level. I’m always happy to sample Dutch oven desserts”, said Tripp with a smile. After doing dishes and packing Scouts enter the Talus Caves formed by tumbled boulders. Scouts descend safely on the trail from the peak to the reservoir. Morgan Bishop, Gianni Richmond, Henry Call, Landon Heppner, Sammy Ragones and Connor Fredericks rest on the trail. A California condor with a 9-foot wingspan scans for signs of a carcass. In 1987, there were only 22 in existence in the world. Of the current population of 505 including those in the captive breeding program, 85 live in the wild at Pinnacles National Park. 10th and 11th-grade Scouts Nate Woodley (left), Schuyler Sawicki, Romi Bhatia, Jack Gross-Whitaker and Corbin Breeden chat while dinner is cooking.

articles.text: Highlanders earns No. 1 seed in Div. 4 NCS post-season playoffs Piedmont’s boys’ soccer team completed its regular season undefeated in league and was awarded the No. 1 seed in Div. 4 in the North Coast Section playoffs. They capped off their schedule with two strong wins, defeating Alameda 2-0 on the road on Wednesday, February 9, and shutting out Encinal 6-0 on Senior Night on Friday, February 11. The team also gained a win by forfeit against San Leandro on Saturday, February 12. Photo by Bill Malecki Piedmont honored its 14 seniors on Friday at Senior Night: (Front row) Adi Kisieu (left), Theo Markopolous, Luis Somers, Ethan Lim, Andre Stankiewicz, Jason Machle, Conner Curtis; (back) Omri Kariv, Arjun Silverberg, Darius Grammer, Ian Work, Anders Payne, Patrick Alexandre, and Jackson Thornborrow. The batch of games brings Piedmont’s overall record to 12-2-3 (12 wins, 2 ties, and 3e losses), and a perfect 10-0-0 against Shoreline Division teams for the second year in a row. Last season, the WACC did not award league banners, though PHS was also 10-0-0. On Senior Night at Witter Field, the team honored its 14 seniors: Arjun Silverberg, Patrick Alexandre, Darius Grammer, Luis Somers, Conner Curtis, Jason Machle, Andre Stankiewicz, Theo Markopoulos, Ethan Lim, Adi Kisieu, Anders Payne, Ian Work, Omri Kariv, and Jackson Thornborrow. Piedmont steps into the Division 4 North Coast Section brackets as the top-dog with the No. 1 seed and a first-round bye. The Highlanders will host the winner of No. 8 Justin-Siena and No. 9 San Domenico on Friday or Saturday, February 18-19. 2-0 win over Alameda The match was scoreless at halftime, 0-0, with the Hornets controlling the game after with several missed scoring opportunities and 10 corner kicks yielding nothing. All of them were starting “We played great; some really good stuff,” said coach Dan Chubbock after the victory over Castro Valley. “We started all nine seniors and they played really well. Honestly, we were the better team. We possessed the ball well, we looked comfortable and we created chances.” Their 3-0 shutout over the Trojans was a good way to move toward North Coast Section playoffs. This is the most resilient team I’ve had and I couldn’t be prouder. We had two starters out, and our bench was great. It feels like every game with O’Dowd has to be a nailbiter,” said Spencer. It was an epic fourth quarter comeback by Piedmont. They trailed 63-41 at the start of the last quarter, but rallied to outscore the Dragons 30-8 and force overtime. Senior captain JoJo Murphy converted three free throws with 1.8 seconds left to force OT and knocked down a 3-pointer at the buzzer at the end of the first overtime period. “This year, we’ve been down before and we always keep fighting. We got stops, got buckets, we just kept fighting. Our seniors really stepped up, it was nothing new seeing everyone give their all,” said Murphy, who finished with 38 points and converted 18 of 19 free throw attempts. It ties his career high in points scored. articles.text: Trinity Zamora named Co-Player of the Year Piedmont’s girls’ basketball team lost a heartbreaker 59-56 in overtime at San Leandro on Friday, February 11, and the Pirates won the Foothill Division champion, It was the first time in the league’s 10-year history that Bishop O’Dowd did not win the title. “We didn’t value the ball and had some empty possessions. Too many turnovers down the stretch. But I’m proud of the girls. It was a hard fought game and hard fought season,” said coach Bryan Gardere now in his 19th season. Two days earlier, February 9, the Highlanders demolished O’Dowd 53-37 In front of a home court crowd on Senior Night in Piedmont. Seniors Hannah Govert and Aniya Perine were honored. The finished with another 20-win season (20-5 overall, 8-2 in league). Although 2021/2022 marked the first time PHS defeated Bishop O’Dowd twice in a season, it was the first time San Leandro ever defeated the Highlanders and O’Dowd. The Pirates also beat Piedmont 50-49 on January 21. Piedmont forced overtime Staff Photo Natalia Martinez scored a 3-pointer at the buzzer to force overtime against San Leandro. PHS honored seniors Hannah Govert and Aniya Perine (not pictured) on Senior Night. thanks to a last second 3-pointer by sophomore Natalia Martinez, releasing her shot as the clock ran out. “We run those plays all the time in practice and we finally got to use one, and it worked,” said Gardere. Junior for ward Trinit y Zamora was named the WACC’s Co-Player of the Year alongside San Leandro’s Geriah Bradley, also a junior. Zamora was The Post’s’ Freshman of the Year in 2020, and Sophomore of the Year in 2021. Zamora scored 17 points, and had 10 rebounds and seven blocked shots against San Leandro. San Leandro recap Piedmont was down 12-0 until scoring their first bucket with 3:11 remaining in the first quarter. They trailed 12-8 at the end of the first quarter and were behind 31-23 at halftime. A 3rd quarter rally tied the game at 38-38 to start the fourth period. Martinez’s buzzer-beater made it 50-50 to force overtime, but foul trouble in OT forced both Martinez and junior Maddie Hill off the floor in the late minutes—enabling San Leandro to win 59-56 to claim the league title. In the third quarter, Piedmont scored the first eight points to tie it at 31-31 before San Leandro’s Bradley hit two free throws to go up 33-31. After a free throw by Martinez, Zamora put PHS ahead 34-33 with 2:35 to go for their first lead of the game. There were four lead changes in the finals 2-1/2 minutes. Piedmont surged ahead 47-41 with 4:45 left, but the Pirates scored eight straight points to go ahead 49-47 with 2:20 on the clock. PHS had its chances but had several possessions without scoring. San Leandro missed the second shot of a one-and-one free throw to make it 50-47 with just 2.4 seconds left. PHS threw the ball up-court to Zamora, who kicked the ball out to Martinez for her dramatic 3-pointer. In overtime, San Leandro scored a 3-pointer and never relinquished the lead. The Pirates extended it to 56-52 when Martinez fouled out with 46 seconds

articles.text: Piedmont’s 8th grade Jasper Schuetz (left) placed second at the CCCX race at Fort Ord, while 10th grade rider Matteo Scanu (right) placed third. The Piedmont Mountain Bike Team competed in an unofficial race on Sunday, February 6 at Fort Ord in Monterey. The race was organized by the Central Coast Cyclo Cross (CCCX) Mountain Bike Racing league. The event attracted top clubs from Bay Area high schools, including El Cerrito and Albany. Racers competed on a three-lap course. Piedmont’s best results were in the boys’ age 14-16 category. 8th grader Jasper Schuetz placed second in a time of 1:02:22 in a field of 20 riders, and teammate Matteo Scanu, a PHS sophomore, was third place in 1:03.17. Piedmont first official race will be on Saturday, February 26 at the Exchequer Extravaganza hosted by the Interscholastic Norcal Cycling League at Exchequer Mountain Bike Park in La Grange in Stanislaus County. The course for high school riders will be five miles with 950 feet in elevation gain, while the Junior Development course is 3.3 miles with 641 elevation gain.

articles.text: A retrospective of geometric art by the late William (Bill) Blackwell will be on display at the Piedmont Center for the Arts from noon to 2 p.m. this weekend on Saturday and Sunday, Feb. 19-20, and on Sunday, February 27. An architect by profession with a lifelong love of geometry, Blackwell’s art work consists of large collages of geometric shapes painted in bright colors, mounted on Masonite. He was fascinated by the possibilities of combining basic shapes and colors into dynamic art. Before he passed away in November 2021, Blackwell also was working on a book he tentatively titled Explorations in Geometry, which focuses on the mathematical beauty of plain geometry and its multiple uses in the built environment. In the book’s introduction, Blackwell noted, “Galileo was one of the first modern thinkers to clearly state that the laws of nature are mathematical. In The Assayer, published in 1623, Galileo wrote ‘philosophy is written in this grand book, the universe… It is written in the language of mathematics, and its characters are triangles, circles, and other geometric figures.’” Blackwell’s first book, Geometry in Architecture, was published by John Wiley & Sons in 1983. Geometric art by Bill Blackwell. His art was previously exhibited at Piedmont Center for the Arts in its first year of operation in 2011. Shortly before that he had a large art exhibit at the former Metro Center in downtown Oakland. He also exhibited his art at the Mathematical Science Research Institute at UC Berkeley, the Hearst Gallery at St. Mary’s College in Moraga, and a gallery in Pt. Reyes. Blackwell received his undergraduate degree at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and his master’s degree in architecture at UC Berkeley. During his career, he was employed by the architecture firm Skidmore and Merrill, the San Francisco Redevelopment Agency, and the Bechtel Corporation for 20 years. He is survived by his wife Marjorie of Piedmont.
articles.title: Bill Blackwell retrospective at PCA opens this Sat.

articles.text: Visit San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA) now through March 6 to see Rafael Lozano-Hemmer’s exhibition “Unstable Presence.” Lozano-Hemmer’s exhibit was slated to premiere in Spring 2020 but was delayed until last fall to accommodate COVID safety precautions. The artist, in describing the exhibition’s title, said it’s meant to be a paradox. “Presence is often associated with existence, continuity in time, or material reality. The ‘unstable’ here refers to interaction, improvisation, and performance. The instability brought by participation is welcome, because it allows constant reinterpretation of the work,” Lozano-Hemmer said. The artist works primarily with media and technology to create artwork and holds a degree in chemistry. Many of his works displayed include some aspect of interactivity. “Sometimes I think of media artwork as not so much part of the visual arts, but the performing arts,” he said. “You’ve got a score, but that score gets interpreted by different orchestras in a different way. Sometimes we pretend we’re crystallizing a moment in time, when in fact what the artist wants is for the artwork to have, on the one hand, a decent life, and then an honorable death.” To purchase tickets visit: https://www.sfmoma.org/exhibition/rafael-lozano-hemmer-unstable-presence/ Photo by Edouard Plante-Fréchette Artist Rafael Lozano-Hemmer by one of his works in France. articles.text: Artist Robert Brokl will have an exhibit, “What I’ve Been Up To” at Piedmont Center for the Arts March 5–20. Gallery hours are 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. on Saturdays and Sundays, with an artist’s reception on Sunday, March 13 at 2 p.m. The landscape-themed exhibition features recent paintings (oil and gouache), pastel drawings, and woodblock prints, with Brokl’s reflections of trips to the Southern Sierra Nevadas, the deserts of Death Valley and Anza Borrego, and the Mendocino area of California’s North Coast. It is a visual diary of recent travels, from the austere, spare deserts and the flora and fauna that survive temperature extremes. “What’s also become sadly apparent is how vulnerable these places are to the effects of the changing climate,” he said. “My depictions of vast forests, azure lakes, and minimalist, unspoiled, primordial deserts are “Befores,” and serve as records of these areas from before the 2020 Creek Fire.
articles.title: Robert Brokl brings art show to Piedmont

articles.text: Young People’s Symphony Orchestra (YPSO) will perform its winter concert at First Congregational Church of Berkeley on Saturday, February 26, at 8 p.m. This year marks YPSO’s 85th season and 33rd season under the baton of Maestro David Ramadanoff. More than Over 90 young musicians, ranging in age from 12 to 19, will perform. The concert will include the works of Dmitiri Shostakovich, and two living American composers, Jennifer Higdon and Adolphus Hailstork. The first half of the program will feature Blue Cathedral by Higdon and Epitaph of a Man Who Dreamed by Hailstork. Higdon described her piece as “about deciding if life was going to be about living or about death.” In describing his work, Hailstork said “I believe that African Americans deserve to have the same homage paid to their suffering, and to their glories when they occur, as has happened throughout all of Western history.” The concert was rescheduled from Martin Luther King, Jr. Day, January 17, but was rescheduled due to COVID-19 concerns. Tickets can be purchased by visiting http://www.ypsomusic. org/tickets, or calling the box office at (510) 849-9776.
articles.title: YPSO Winter Concert on February 26

articles.text: San Francisco Symphony is honoring the legacy of music maestro Michael Morgan with a program conceived by the late conductor. Morgan, former Oakland Symphony music director who passed away last year, was originally slated to conduct these performances. Conductors Earl Lee, Daniel Bartholomew-Poyser, and Akiko Fujimoto will lead the program, which will feature mezzo-soprano Melody Wilson and the San Francisco Symphony Chorus. The program includes Carlos Simon’s Amen!, My Soul’s Been Anchored in the Lord, Give Me Jesus, and Come Thou Fount of Every Blessing, and Florence Price’s Symphony No. 3, all San Francisco Symphony premieres. Before his passing in August 2021, Morgan offered his insights on the program. “This concert has a couple of threads running through it. First of all, it’s about religion and spirituality, particularly American, although all the pieces are not American because the ideas are, if not universal, certainly global,” he said. The performances will take place at Davies Symphony Hall in San Francisco on Thursday, Friday and Saturday, February 17-19, All performances are at 7:30 p.m. For more information, including full program notes, visit the San Francisco Symphony website at www.sfsymphony.org, or call the box office at (415) 864-6000 to obtain tickets. Michael Morgan
articles.title: SF Symphony to present Michael Morgan memorial program Feb 17-19

articles.text: San Francisco Ballet will present its production of Don Quixote, with music by Ludwig Minkus and choreography by Alexander Gorksy and Marius Petipa, beginning February 26. Don Quixote, based on the classic novel by Miguel de Cervantes, is filled with physical humor and fiery dancing. Artistic Director Helgi Tomasson said one of the production’s most appealing aspects is “the joy it gives you - you could say it’s a bit of a farce, nothing dramatic or psychological. It’s upbeat and fun.” Don Quixote first took the stage at San Francisco Ballet in 2003, and over the years has been updated by Tomasson since its initial premiere. In 2012, award-winning costume designer Martin Pakledinaz introduced 19th-century Spanish garb and visually striking scenery. In redeveloping the classic story, Paklendinaz, who passed away shortly after the 2012 performance, said “it’s important to drop what you’ve seen and try to make it your original production.” Don Quixote will open at the War Memorial Opera House on Saturday, February 26, at 8 p.m., with performances through March 6. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.sfballet.org/aboutdon-quixote/. Sarah Van Patten in San Francisco Ballet’s production of Don Quixote. Photo by Erik Tomasson
articles.title: SF Ballet presents Don Quixote beginning February 26

Brock is the leading authority of the music of Charlie Chaplin and was selected directly by the Chaplin family to restore all published film scores composed by him, including City Lights. Michael Morgan SF Ballet presents Don Quixote beginning February 26 By Allyson Aleksey San Francisco Ballet will present its production of Don Quixote, with music by Ludwig Minkus and choreography by Alexander Gorksy and Marius Petipa, beginning February 26. Don Quixote, based on the classic novel by Miguel de Cervantes, is filled with physical humor and fiery dancing. Artistic Director Helgi Tomasson said one of the production’s most appealing aspects is “the joy it gives you - you could say it’s a bit of a farce, nothing dramatic or psychological. It’s upbeat and fun.” Don Quixote first took the stage at San Francisco Ballet in 2003, and over the years has been updated by Tomasson since its initial premiere. In 2012, award-winning costume designer Martin Pakledinaz introduced 19th-century Spanish garb and visually striking scenery. In redeveloping the classic story, Paklendinaz, who passed away shortly after the 2012 performance, said “it’s important to drop what you’ve seen and try to make it your original production.” Don Quixote will open at the War Memorial Opera House on Saturday, February 26, at 8 p.m., with performances through March 6. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.sfballet.org/aboutdon-quixote/. Sarah Van Patten in San Francisco Ballet’s production of Don Quixote. More than Over 90 young musicians, ranging in age from 12 to 19, will perform. The concert will include the works of Dmitiri Shostakovich, and two living American composers, Jennifer Higdon and Adolphus Hailstork. The first half of the program will feature Blue Cathedral by Higdon and Epitaph of a Man Who Dreamed by Hailstork. Higdon described her piece as “about deciding if life was going to be about living or about death.” In describing his work, Hailstork said “I believe that African Americans deserve to have the same homage paid to their suffering, and to their glories when they occur, as has happened throughout all of Western history.” The concert was rescheduled from Martin Luther King, Jr. Day, January 17, but was rescheduled due to COVID-19 concerns. Timothy Brock will lead the Symphony for this event which is dedicated to the memory of the late conductor Michael Morgan. Brock is the leading authority of the music of Charlie Chaplin and was selected directly by the Chaplin family to restore all published film scores composed by him, including City Lights. articles.text: Annette Bening and Julianne Moore star in The Kids Are All Right. The Kids Are All Right is a film about family: parents, two teenage kids, a spacious home in a generic part of Southern California, and, in the establishing scenes, a nice way of all living together. As it turns out, the parents are two women, Jules (Julianne Moore) and Nic (Annette Bening), a married couple who share a bond of love and commitment with one another and with their children and have created a wonderful, ordinary, quirky, and slightly dysfunctional family. What is nicely brilliant about this film is that though the audience is aware that the moms are lesbians, that fact soon becomes irrelevant, as unimportant as a straight couple being thought of as heterosexual. Assume that there are countless families from coast to coast that fit this family’s profile and then accept that love and support and familial dissonance has nothing to do with sexual identity but is, simply, a matter of our fundamental humanity. This reality makes the strident resistance to same sex marriage (and gays in the military) seem hurtful and unnecessary and downright bigoted, not to mention unconstitutional. It’s a truth embedded in every frame of “The Kids Are All Right,” though it is never mentioned. Thankfully, the writers, director Lisa Cholodenko and Stuart Blumberg, allow the screenplay to show and not tell. So, given that the Jules/Nic family, like all families, is ordinary and extraordinary, has its own rhythms, routines, tics and familiar ways of interacting, it’s a given that if a stranger is inserted into this emotional ecology, well, sit back and wait for the disruption. And therein is the dramatic and comedic thread that stitches this story together. Older daughter, Joni (Mia Wasikowska), 18, on the cusp of going away to college, is urged by her younger brother, Laser (Josh Hutcherson), to find their sperm-donor father, Paul (Mark Ruffolo). Remarkably, she is able to track him down and, in an interesting phone conversation, explain that she and Laser would like to meet him (without Jules and Nic being aware of what they are doing). And so Paul, a motorcycle-riding bachelor, restaurateur, who raises organic vegetables, is introduced into the family dynamic, to the initial shock of the two moms. Surprise! Dad’s home. The familial gyroscope becomes a bit wobbly, and then a lot wobbly. What was a familiar and nice mess of a family, content in its small dysfunctions, is now forced to make new and comedic and dramatic adjustments, meaning lots of information and interactions need to be, in Nic’s words, “processed.” Actually when Jules and Nic interact with each other, and with the kids, it’s as if all the pop psych language that sprouted in the 60s, and burnished over the last 40 years, is now de rigueur as they strive to be sensitive to and open with their children, often asking for, and giving, way too much information (TMI). Some of the dialogue sounds a bit hackneyed (“Sometimes you hurt the one you love”). Thankfully, Nic didn’t insist that “love means never having to say you’re sorry.” The performances are just about perfect. Benning and Moore are deeply talented actors who inhabit their characters with power and charm and comedic timing. Some scenes are extraordinary. Ruffalo is ideally cast as the outsider who is trying to understand where he might fit in this familial diorama while never quite finding his balance. If the film is flawed, it’s in its ending. Without discussing in detail the conclusion, it seems a bit cold and abrupt, especially given the efforts that Jules and Nic make throughout to “process” their feelings and nurture their relationships. That aside, the film is joyful, stuffed like a sausage with all manner of interesting and even compelling moments that reflect, in so many ways, the challenges of living in a family. The Kids Are All Right. Directed by Lis Cholodenko. Starring Annette Bening, Mark Ruffalo, Julianne Moore, Mia Wasikowska and Josh Hutcherson. 2 hrs., 29 min. Rated R.

articles.text: Matthew McConaughey and Djimon Hounsou star in Amistad. After watching the remarkable film, Amistad, released in 1997, and directed by Steven Spielberg, I was aware that February is Black History month. The film is a powerful narrative that asks us to pause and contemplate the nature of myopic, incomprehensible cruelty, not unlike Spielberg’s Schindler’s List, a story about the Holocaust. It is summer of 1839 off the coast of Cuba when 53 men, imprisoned on the Spanish slave ship La Amistad, escape and kill all their guards with the exception of two, who they insist turn the ship head east and take them back to Africa. Instead the slave traders trick the men on board, led by Çinque (Djimon Mounson), and head up the eastern seaboard where it is eventually captured by a naval warship not far from the coast of Connecticut. The Africans are shackled and imprisoned, and charged with murder and piracy. And thus begins a trial, wherein the 53 men are initially represented by abolitionists Roger Baldwin (Matthew McConaughey) and Lewis Tappan (Stellan Skarsgard) and later John Quincy Adams (Anthony Hopkins). The defense argued that the Africans were not property, but free men who were kidnapped, and should be returned to their country of origin. Ultimately, the trial asks the fundamental question: how is it possible to regard human beings as chattel, not only taken against their will, but sold, traded, and worked, often to death, with impunity. In other words how do we comprehend the existence of slavery? The essence of this powerfully told story attempts to not only define the meaning of humanity, but challenges the pious rationale that supported the economic institution of slavery and its profound immorality. What Amistad makes clear is the power of film to depict injustice, racism, prejudice and what proved to be a form of lethal discrimination, later referred to as Jim Crow. But instead of analyzing further the meaning of this extraordinary moment in history, let me suggest other examples (all now streaming) from our past that filmmakers have turned to as they examined evil and the human condition. Consider viewing A Time to Kill, Just Mercy, Hidden Figures, Mississippi Burning, Remember the Titans, Guess Who is Coming to Dinner, 12 Years a Slave, Selma, The Birth of a Nation, King in the Wilderness, When They See Us, and 13th. Without doubt, the films listed above can change the human heart as well as alter our historical perspective. Amistad. Directed by Steven Spielberg. Starring Morgan Freeman, Anthony Hopkins, Matthew McConaughey. 2 hrs., 32 min. Rated R.
articles.title: Amistad a powerful story of slave ships

articles.text: The first Iron Man movie was released in 2008. It had a high “wow factor” to be sure. It was fresh and interesting, a shiny adaptation of the Marvel Comics’ character, Iron Man, brought to life by the talented actor Robert Downey. Iron Man 1 delivered the necessary backstory regarding how Iron Man came to be, along with the astonishing technology that turned Tony Stark, industrialist, into a high-flying weapons system. The Iron Man suit defines cool. Plus, it’s always a thrill watching a superhero’s history unfold, watching as he or she begins to take control of newly discovered and unexpected abilities. Recall Superman, arriving on earth in the center of a meteor; or Spider Man, bitten by a spider, grappling with his metamorphosis. It’s a rush. Hence, that first Iron Man movie, now in franchise mode, was superb entertainment. The challenge then was how to craft a sequel that would be equally gripping. Comic book adaptations have become an entertainment staple using familiar characters Batman, Hulk, X-Men, Superman, Spider Man, Hellboy, to name a few. Which brings us to Iron Man 2. To be certain creating a sequel can be problematical. For writer Justin Theroux and director Don Favreau, the trick was to find a story that presented a now established Tony Stark aka Iron Man in a new and interesting way. Plus, a new antagonist had to be introduced, an opponent worthy of Stark’s incomparable strength, wealth and intelligence. If not done well and with real imagination, the filmmakers risked “jumping the shark,” meaning that the Iron Man 1 narrative had peaked with the first film and anything thereafter would be predictable and anti-climactic. The term “jump the shark” is most often used to describe the moment when a TV series or movie franchise begins its downturn and things spin off into absurdity. The intensity and crispness of the first movie (or Mickey Rourke plays the villian, Ivan Vanko (Whiplash), in Iron Man 2. first season in television) has been dulled, the story has lost its edge and the originality, which made the initial premise appealing, is missing. The film has devolved into the formulaic. In an effort to make Stark extraordinary and more complex, the writers make him decidedly un-heroic. He’s arrogant, hubristic, and seemingly consumed with his newfound fame and power. No surprise, he’s not very appealing. In one scene he arrives before a government oversight committee with studied insouciance, flashing the peace sign, declaring world peace has been privatized, while displaying an ego that is in need of deflating. Though watching Robert Downey portray even clippings from a phone book is always a treat, this second incarnation of Stark in which the screenwriter goes for comic relief is strange. And entirely unnecessary. Downey is a consummate actor as is Gwyneth Paltrow as Pepper Potts, his unacknowledged love interest and solidly competent girl Friday. As for Mickey Roark, in all his grungy splendor, well, he’s passable as a Russian named Ivan Vanko, wingnut scientist, and Stark’s bad dude nemesis. Samuel L. Jackson makes an appearance, briefly, as Nick Fury as does Scarlett Johansson in the role of Natalie, aka Black Widow. The burden that any sequel carries is one of story. Once Iron Man’s history has been revealed, and his superhero talents established, it all comes down to imagination. Does Iron Man 2 have the right stuff? The answer is no. The hardware is wonderful. The suit is still a treat to watch: wax on, wax off. But the rest, the loud climactic battle, the flights at supersonic speeds, all of it is familiar. Fall back position: craft a great screenplay. Otherwise, as B.B. King’s song explains, the thrill is gone. Iron Man 2. Directed by Jon Favreau. Starring Robert Downey, Don Cheadle, Gwyneth Paltrow, Scarlett Johansson and Mickey Rourke. 2 hrs., 4 min. Rated PG-13.
articles.title: MOVIES FOR KIDS Iron Man 2 – the thrill is gone

articles.text: Nathan Lane and Lee Evans in Mousehunt. Mouse Hunt, released in 1997, is a family friendly film that kids and their parents will thoroughly enjoy. Think of it as a manic riff on Home Alone, or reminiscent of the slapstick comedy of Laurel and Hardy and the Three Stooges. It’s a hoot, and both Nathan Lane, in the role of Ernie Smultz, and Lee Evans as Lars Smultz, are both exceptional in their respective roles as bumbling siblings whose niche is: whatever can go wrong will go wrong – in a most hilarious way. The plot of the story goes something like this: Ernie and Lars have inherited from their recently deceased father an abandoned Victorian mansion. Dad has also left them a string factory that they discover is in some financial difficulty. The two conclude that they need some cash, and the best thing to do is fix up the big old house and sell it, sooner than later. As circumstances would have it, the brothers find that they have to spend a night in the fixer-upper, and it’s then that they discover the place has a lone resident – A Mouse (CGI) – just one singular occupant. But they know that a rodent, even this little guy, could impact the possible sale of the house and so it has to go. What follows are the brothers plotting and planning a series of outrageous, very ineffective mousetraps, all of them involving sustained mayhem. The two bros even buy a monster feline cat they name Catzella, for the sole purpose of joining the hunt, but to no avail. So desperate are they that they hire a wacky exterminator called Caesar (Christopher Walken), who takes on the challenge and is pretty much a disaster waiting to happen. Meanwhile, it becomes clear that the mouse manages to outsmart everyone who attempts to catch it. In other words, he is one bright little rodent. Even Lars, at his wits end, chases the little fellow through the house with a shotgun, managing only to blow a hole in the floor. It’s all wonderful fun. Kids, tweens and teens will have a great time as they root for the mouse. Mouse Hunt. Directed by Gore Verbinski. Starring Nathan Lane, Lee Evans and Vicki Lewis. 1 hr., 37 min. Rated PG. Streaming on HBO.

articles.text: Reflections on dissent It was a slow day at the office. The mind began to wander. I can hear my father’s voice saying, “Get to work.” So, here it is. A noted philosopher once said, “From the genius we learn what to do. From the fool we learn what not to do.” Keeping this philosophy in mind, let’s see where it leads us. First, we must remember the two most important aspects of music; the technical and the emotional. A logical equilibrium must be maintained, with neither aspect overpowering the other. All technique without the leavening of emotion is barren. The opposite is equally true. Every great composer knew this formula; either innately or learned along the way. Modern performers have lost their way as interpreters. When it comes to technique, I always call on the great football coach Vince Lombardi. He addressed every aspect of technique when he said, “The team that controls the line of scrimmage wins the game.” He always insisted on respect. The emotional aspect of music was addressed by the important American violinist Albert Spalding. He didn’t use the word “respect”; he used another word that was equally meaningful. “The keynote to artistic worth is: Sincerity. Sincerity. Sincerity. All other qualities relate to it, and are valueless without it.” A third musical philosopher might seem out of place, but I am adding Napoleon Bonaparte. I have found that the greatest composers use the orchestra in the same way that Napoleon used his “Old Guard”. Napoleon used his old guard in a strategic way, saving the great climax for the most opportune time. Dissent is not new to music. Composers, performers, audiences, and critics have rarely agreed. Here is an example from the 1830s showing Franz Liszt (left) and Sigismund Thalberg, two of the most famous concert performers of the age engaged in a musical duel.

articles.text: All public events at Piedmont Center for the Arts require photo ID and valid proof of vaccination, including booster shot, for entry, as well as proper masking while inside. Saturday, February 19, 12 noon – 2 p.m. Blackwell art exhibit William Blackwell, a prominent architect who once created and published a unique world map centered on the Bay Area, was also a furniture maker and artist, and a Piedmont resident since 1980 until he recently passed away. pages.text: 20 Wednesday, February 16, 2022 The Musical Gourmet Reflections on dissent By Joseph Gold It was a slow day at the office. The mind began to wander. I can hear my father’s voice saying, “Get to work.” So, here it is. A noted philosopher once said, “From the genius we learn what to do. From the fool we learn what not to do.” Keeping this philosophy in mind, let’s see where it leads us. First, we must remember the two most important aspects of music; the technical and the emotional. A logical equilibrium must be maintained, with neither aspect overpowering the other. All technique without the leavening of emotion is barren. The opposite is equally true. Every great composer knew this formula; either innately or learned along the way. Modern performers have lost their way as interpreters. When it comes to technique, I always call on the great football coach Vince Lombardi. He addressed every aspect of technique when he said, “The team that controls the line of scrimmage wins the game.” He always insisted on respect. The emotional aspect of music was addressed by the important American violinist Albert Spalding. He didn’t use the word “respect”; he used another word that was equally meaningful. “The keynote to artistic worth is: Sincerity. Sincerity. Sincerity. All other qualities relate to it, and are valueless without it.” A third musical philosopher might seem out of place, but I am adding Napoleon Bonaparte. I have found that the greatest composers use the orchestra in the same way that Napoleon used his “Old Guard”. Napoleon used his old guard in a strategic way, saving the great climax for the most opportune time. Contrast that with what I call The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet “the Hollywood Blast”. Hollywood film scores are characterized by a continual blast of volume no matter what the music is. It is a casualty of the age. My first violin teacher related the advice of the illustrious violin virtuoso Sarasate, who advised economy of motion at all times. Such advice was used by almost all of the great performers. The great operatic tenor Tito Schipa was convinced that there was better communication with less body English – more control also. These great artists were interested in impressing intelligent audiences. Here again, sincerity and respect emerge as the artistic ideal. The immortal Paganini touched the souls of his audiences more with his profundity then with his technical virtuosity. His expressive tone brought listeners to tears. He never stooped to cheap theatrics. Everything he did was designed to communicate the highest artistic level. The great artists of the past painted music with a multi-hued pallet. They drew their audiences in and made them part of the action. My own professor, Jascha Heifetz, was never known as a raconteur. But he always expressed himself in the most straightforward and succinct terms. He didn’t use lots of words, but what he said always rang true. And he didn’t always have great things to say about music critics. Heifetz might have concluded this article by saying: the above is a brief history lesson. It is skewed a little bit… but not too much. And so, what can we learn from history? Dissent forces us to reflect. These opposing forces are a dichotomy which can be presented in three sentences: A contemporary critic tells us that “It’s all showbiz. Hooray for the glitz!” I am convinced that we must look behind the superficial glitz – that’s where the real quality resides. Dissent is not new to music. Composers, performers, audiences, and critics have rarely agreed. Here is an example from the 1830s showing Franz Liszt (left) and Sigismund Thalberg, two of the most famous concert performers of the age engaged in a musical duel.
