articles.text: Piedmont High School alumnus Sara Dosa, class of 2000, premiered her newest documentary, Fire of Love, at the 2022 Sundance Film Festival, selected as one of five films in the documentary category. The documentary was picked up for theatrical distribution by National Geographic following the premiere. Dosa is an Indie Spirit Award-nominated director and Peabody award-winning producer, whose film credits include Audrie & Daisy, available on at-home streaming service Netflix, The Seer and the Unseen, and The Last Season. Fire of Love, Dosa’s documentary chronicling the work of Maurice and Katia Krafft, French husband-wife volcanologists, opened the Sundance Film Festival on January 20. The film contains over 20 years of archival footage and dramatic shots of active volcanoes and explosions. The Krafft couple traveled to volcanic locations in Zaire, Iceland, the Americas and Japan, capturing then-unseen footage of seismic, tectonic eruptions. The footage came into Dosa’s hands when directing The Seer and the Unseen in Iceland in 2019. Finding what the couple captured as “extraordinary and provoking,” she pursued a documentary based solely on the couple. “It was like a puzzle, stitching together over two decades of archival footage, and these incredible moments Maurice and Katia captured,” she said. Under her direction, the team behind Fire of Love weaved the Piedmont documentary film director and producer Sara Dosa. footage together to tell the couple’s love story. The Kraffts spent decades collecting data mere feet away from danger. In 1991 they were killed capturing an explosion on Japan’s Mount Unzen. They left behind a legacy and some of the most dramatic footage humans may ever be able to capture. “I like to think of it as a love triangle. Maurice and Katia were obviously the love story that drove [the narrative], but you also have the volcanoes they chased. In a way they were both in love with this important work they did,” Dosa said. As director, Dosa was involved with every stage of the film, including in the documentary’s clever use of animation and in writing the copy provided to Miranda July, author and independent film screenwriter, who narrates the film. Dosa said she consulted with the Krafft’s contemporaries and colleagues when considering what story to tell - but that the bulk of the narration comes directly from the footage the couple captured, and the Krafft’s own notes, speeches and published works. “I wanted to make something that, if they were able to see it, they would consider an accurate and compelling portrayal of their lives,” Dosa said. Bidding for the film began shortly after its premiere, with streaming giants like Netflix, Sony Pictures, National Geographic, IFC, Universal, and Amazon all included. The deal for Fire of Love closed late last month, with National Geographic Documentary Films closing a mid-seven-figure worldwide rights deal. Volcanologists Maurice and Katia Krafft, the subjects of a documentary film by Piedmont alum Sara Dosa.

articles.text: Photos courtesy of Columbus Zoo Captain Cal experienced complications stemming from a California wildfire in 2020. Captain Cal, one of three mountain lions rescued from the devastating Zogg and August Complex fires near Redding in September 2020 and transported to Oakland Zoo, experienced additional complications due to burns sustained. On February 4 he had several toes amputated by Columbus Zoo in Ohio, where he has been cared for since November 2020. Captain Cal came to Oakland Zoo in 2020 as a severely burned orphaned male mountain lion cub, and is named after the firefighters that rescued him. He made a promising recovery after 47 days of intensive care at Oakland Zoo’s veterinary hospital and under the care of the California Department of Fish &Wildlife (CDFW). He was transported to Columbus Zoo after receiving roundthe-clock care, daily bandage changes, pain medication, antibiotics, and surgery that partially amputated his toes. Captain Cal recovers from a four-hour procedure that removed several of his toes. Dr. Brittany Carson performs surgery on Captain Cal. Columbus Zoo announced that the cougar, now fully grown, experienced some new complications due to the injuries he sustained from the fire. While he has been doing well overall, his previous injuries from being trapped in the wildlife fires continued to cause challenges. Dr. Brittany Carson, a surgeon at Ohio State University’s College of Veterinary Medicine, said the decision was made to partially amputate the tips of several more of Captain Cal’s toes. The procedure took approximately 4 hours, and he was then transported to the Zoo’s Animal Health Center to be monitored. “WE PAY YOUR SALES TAX”* *On all installed jobs

articles.text: I don’t remember which year exactly it was when I discovered Beekeeper – maybe 10 years ago. I was at the annual Zinfandel Advocates and Producers (ZAP) tasting in San Francisco. In those days this was one of the largest wine tastings in the country – a huge array of big teeth-staining wines. It takes a lot to stand out in an array of so many powerful wines, but at the end of the day there was one wine that truly stood out from the crowd – Beekeeper. The winery was just getting started and founder Ian Blackburn had made only a few cases. Blackburn went on to partner with Clay Mauritson whose family owns some magnificent vineyards in the Rockpile AVA and production today is under 900 cases. The Beekeeper philosophy is simple: treat Zinfandel with the same respect as Cabernet Sauvignon, the king of California grapes. Grapes are selected from only the finest vineyards and yields are kept low. The wines are aged in mostly new French oak barrels which helps explain the prices. In other words – it’s the royal treatment. It doesn’t hurt that Blackburn and Mauritson are talented winemakers who learn and adapt from each new vintage. Beekeeper is able to pull off a tough task. The wines are big, full-bodied and powerful, yet they are not ponderous or tiring on the palate. They possess exquisite balance which keeps them refreshing despite their size. They are also some of the few Zinfandels that actually improve with age, and I recommend a few years in the cellar before serving. The best way to acquire the wines is through the website www.beekeepercellars.com. pull out to serve with leg of lamb or a pork crown roast. • 2018 Beekeeper Zinfandel Montecillo Vineyard, $75 The Rockpile AVA in a remote corner of Sonoma country is a relatively recent appellation but it has proven itself to be able to produce outstanding Zinfandels. This wine is a good example. Deep ruby/purple, with a stunning nose of anise, jasmine, blueberry, blackberry jam and earth, the wine is majestic, full-bodied and an absolute tour de force in Zinfandel winemaking. It should drink well for at least 10 years. • 2018 Beekeeper Zinfandel Hidden Hillside Reserve, $75 This wine is a blend of three vineyards and is made only in select vintages. It is blended with 4% Petite Sirah for added structure. It offers up superb notes of black fruits, licorice, pepper, and flowers. With amazing concentration, an opulent, full-bodied palate, and fabulous length, the wine shows why Beekeeper is in a class of its own in the world of Zinfandel. Would love to drink this with a hearty beef stew or cassoulet. 2018 Beekeeper Zinfandel Secret Stones, $85 This wine from the Rockpile AVA (Sonoma Valley) comes from a vineyard at 1500 feet in elevation. It is blended with 3% Petite Sirah. It sports loads of black raspberry, kirsch liqueur, lavender, anise, and subtle earthy notes in this multidimensional, full-bodied, gloriously decadent and tasty Zinfandel. Lay this baby down for a few years then • Beekeeper Cellars’ 2018 Zinfandel Hidden Hillside Reserve. ®

articles.text: First Mondays Reading Group members: Mike Henn, Nancy Henn, Ken Young, Melba Yee, Sarah Johnson, Alicia Rivera, Laura Goldman, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Pat McMahon, Albert Chen, Adriene Hamlin, Bella Almanzan, Dick Carter, Priscilla Wanerus, Carol Long, and first-time participants Darby and Jerry Gragg. The Piedmont Recreation Department’s First Mondays Reading Group met outside the Tea House in the Piedmont Park on February 7. It was a warm, sunny afternoon that had members of the group looking for shade under the park’s tall redwood trees in this beautiful setting. It was hard to believe that cool weather a month before had caused them to have their January discussion as a Zoom call. Seventeen readers were in attendance, one of the group’s largest turnouts. Everyone was in the same boat about the New York Times bestseller The Boys in the Boat by Daniel James Brown. They all loved it and found very little to criticize. The Boys in the Boat is about the University of Washington eight-oared crew that represented the United States in the 1936 Olympic Games in Berlin. It is a true story based on the struggles and sacrifices made by the rowers to compete in the Olympics, and how they narrowly beat Italy and Germany to win the gold medal. The eight young men who won gold had experienced significant hardships in their early lives. All of them came from poorer, rural areas, and started their educations during the Great Depression. However, their determination, rigorous training, and dedicated coaches provide them with the strength and ability to win. Brown’s main character is Joe Rantz. As a youth, Joe was abandoned by his father and stepmother because she didn’t want him in her house. Joe was forced live alone in rural Washington, far from relatives, with no family, and little other support. articles.text: As you prepare your tax returns before the April 18 filing deadline, you’ll want to be up to date on changes that could affect you. Here are some issues to discuss with your tax professional: • COVID-19-related distributions and recontributions If you took a coronavirus-related distribution (withdrawal) from a retirement account, such as a 401(k) or IRA, in 2020 and chose to spread the amount equally over three years, you need to include the relevant part of the distribution on your 2021 tax return, so you should bring your 2020 Form 1099-R to your tax advisor. You can recontribute your distributions back into any retirement account eligible to receive a rollover for up to three years after you received the initial distribution. So, if you haven’t already done so, you can still recontribute to your 401(k) or IRA up until the April 18 filing deadline – and by doing so, you could reduce your 2021 taxes. (Your tax professional will know what forms and documentation you’ll need for this recontribution.) • Return of RMDs In 2020, the Coronavirus Aid, Relief and Economic Security (CARES) Act suspended the required minimum distributions (RMDs) from retirement accounts that people over a certain age typically must take. But RMDs returned for 2021 and had to be taken by Dec. 31, unless your birthdate is between July 1 and Dec. 31, 1949, in which case your starting date was delayed until April 1, 2022. So, if you had an RMD for 2021, bring your 2020 Form 5498 or your 2021 retirement account statements to your tax professional to calculate the required RMD. You’ll also want to provide your 2021 Form 1099-R to report the amount of RMDs taken. • Charitable contributions The CARES Act authorized a deduction for cash contributions to qualified charities for those who don’t itemize. For 2020, the maximum deduction was $300; this provision has been extended for the 2021 tax year, with a new provision allowing a $600 deduction for joint filers. If you do itemize deductions, be aware that the CARES Act also suspended the 60% of adjusted gross income limit for cash gifts in 2020, a change that has been carried over to 2021. • Child tax credit For 2021, you can claim up to $3,600 for children younger than 6 and up to $3,000 for children ages 6 to 17. This tax credit is refundable, which means you can receive it even if it’s larger than the amount of taxes you owe. The credit phases out at certain income limits. • Child and dependent care credit This credit is more substantial in 2021 – up to $4,000 for one qualifying person and up to $8,000 for two or more. This credit is also potentially refundable, but it phases out differently than in previous years, so you’ll want to go over your dependent-care expenses carefully with your tax professional. And last, but certainly not least, review your IRA contributions. There aren’t any changes for 2022, but you can still fund your traditional or Roth IRA for the 2021 tax year up until the April 18 deadline. to ensure you’ve got everything in order. Staffing shortages at the Internal Revenue Service (IRS), combined with a heavy workload due to pandemic-related programs, may slow down processing of returns, so consider getting your taxes done as soon as possible – especially if you’re anticipating a refund. articles.text: Independence is something that becomes so intrinsic to most people after early childhood that it can be a shock to lose some independence with age or illness. In the United States, in contrast to many other countries, independence is highly valued. The Pew Research Center found that “nearly four-in-ten older adults around the world live with extended family, but those in the U.S. rarely do.” Their study also includes the following details: “In the U.S., 27% of adults ages 60 and older live alone, compared with 16% of adults in the 130 countries and territories studied. In many countries in the Asia-Pacific, sub-Saharan Africa and the Middle East, fewer than 5% of seniors live alone.” Simply put, older people live in smaller households. “U.S. adults ages 60 and older also are more likely than their counterparts around the world to live as a couple without young children at home.” The reasons for this choice can be economic and based on government services available to older adults, as well as cultural norms. However, there can be benefits to asking for help as you maintain independence too. How home care can support independence Despite this preference for living alone, as people age and their abilities change, so too does the need for support. In-home care services can help individuals develop a life of interdependence while maintaining independence in their everyday lives. Starting with the idea of “aging in place”, which means living in one’s home and not a facility, a representative from a home care agency can come in to do a falls risk assessment. and reducing the risk of a fall, someone who is living alone at an advanced age might be able to enjoy independence longer. A caregiver can help with light housekeeping, decluttering and removing any tripping hazards, and point out areas of risk to be addressed by a professional electrician, plumber or handyman. For example, the caregiver may be aware that someone is getting up frequently at night to use the bathroom and also observe an absence of nightlights to guide the way. Simply having a caregiver to engage with regularly to provide companionship, assist with recovering from a surgery, do some meal preparation, give rides to and from medical appointments, can help a senior to stay sharp, feel less lonely and therefore able to stay more independent. This Senior Independence Month, look at ways to prolong independence for yourself or a loved one, and also consider embracing interdependence with home care services and caregiving. articles.text: Oakland’s rock star biologist Damon Tighe is the headliner for a free-to-the-public “Topics of Merritt” speaker series at Lake Merritt – Independent Senior Living on March 10 at 3:30 p.m. “We are so happy to offer an encore appearance by this charming biotechnologist and urban naturalist who has been featured on local news programs and articles,” said Tim Johnson. For this “Topics of Merritt” program, Tighe will present “Fish and Friends of Lake Merritt’s Waters.” He will also highlight the fact that salmon are finding their way back into the Lake Merritt watershed. He speaker series is designed to offer Lake Merritt Senior Living residents and a wider audience access to some of the most interesting and compelling speakers from the community and beyond. Since its inception, “Topics of Merritt” has featured Dr. Jill Tarter of the SETI program and the scientist at the center of the movie Contact; San Francisco Chronicle Theater Critic Lily Janiak; international ballerina Stephanie Herman who performed with Nureyev; and renowned chefs explaining how to cook more healthy meals. As for Tighe’s upcoming talk, it seems that Chinook salmon numbering in the hundreds have been seen since late fall in East Bay rivers and streams that lead to Lake Merritt. Oakland residents have reported sightings in the lake near Glen Echo where the creek runs alongside the Veterans Memorial Building, as well as a tributary that begins in the Oakland hills near Mountain View Cemetery and empties into the northwest branch of the lake near the intersection of Grand Avenue and Harrison Street. Chinook salmon have not been Oakland biologist Damon Tighe will speak on March 10 at Lake Merritt – Independent Senior Living, to talk about the wildlife found at Lake Merritt. seen in the lake for more than 20 years. Once prevalent in Lake Merritt, salmon typically don’t survive in the area due to manmade culverts and pollution. Volunteer groups have been helping provide a healthy fish habitat. The Lake Merritt Institute partners with local citizens and Oakland school students to clean up Lake Merritt’s shoreline and creeks on a weekly basis. Conservationists say these salmon sightings in the lake highlight the much-needed care that goes into conserving Lake Merritt’s amazing but fragile ecosystem. A local conservation expert, Tighe attended Saint Mary’s College in Moraga where he worked on local newspapers while earning a degree in Biology and Chemistry. He taught high school in Portland, Oregon before moving back to the Bay Area to work on the Human Genome Project at the National Lab’s Joint Genome Institute. He also spent time pursuing an MFA in Natural History and Science Filmmaking in Montana but returned to Oakland to work on single cell genomics. He now teaches biotechnology to high school teachers through Bio-Rad Laboratories and is well versed in local fungi, plants and the critters of Lake Merritt. The public is invited to join a free Zoom presentation on March 10. To register, click on: www. tinyurl.com/lakemerrittfish. Tim Johnson is Executive Director of The Lake Merritt - Independent Senior Living, 1800 Madison Street, Oakland. For information, call 510-903-3600 or visit www.thelakemerritt.com.

Dear MacMama: I have my photos all over the place! Some on my iPhone, some on my iMac, some on my laptop. My son said that I should use iCloud for my photos. He also said that I should use it for my contacts and calendars and my files. How does that work? Jess G., Oakland Dear Jess: This problem with too much stuff and too many devices holding that stuff is such a common issue, that I would say 75% of my on-site work is helping people synchronize their photos, calendars, and contacts. These days, the current iPhones have such great cameras that we just are inspired to take lots of pictures! Each time we get a new computer or device, we do our best to move our data over from our old machines. So many of us have photos that go back to the early 2000s if not earlier. Wouldn’t be great if there was a way to make all our photos sync with each of our devices? Well of course, there is! If you enable iCloud for Photos on all of your devices, they will eventually sync and be stored in the cloud and show up on all devices with iCloud enabled. So, let’s say you take a picture with your iPhone, it will show up on your laptop, your iMac, your iPad; any device that has iCloud enabled for Photos. Of course, you must be signed into the same Apple ID on all of the devices, have iCloud enabled for Photos on all of them which will then allow all of your stuff to sync. Many clients worry that with so many photos your hard drive will get full too quickly. Especially if you have a small one, like 256 GB or even 128 GB. When you choose to enable iCloud in your photos, you have the option of storing a smaller version of the photos on your device, and then you can always download the full version if you want to print it. I use the word “eventually” it will all sync because if you have a large photo library with videos, let’s say for example on your iMac, it can take quite a while to upload to the cloud. And it all depends on the speed of your Internet. If you haven’t reasonably fast Internet connection, even if you have a huge photo library, it can pretty much all be done within a day. The one caveat is that if you are using the free version of iCloud (5GB), it’s very likely you will have to pay to increase your storage. But I find a price to be very reasonable, up to 50 GB is $.99 a month, and up to 200 GB is $2.99 a month. If you need even more space, you can upgrade to 2 TB of storage for $9.99 a month. You also can also use iCloud to store and synchronize your desktop, documents, bookmarks, keychain (which stores passwords) which allows you to access your files from all your devices. You can even access files on your iPhone that live on your desktop. This can be certainly useful if you need to quickly send or print a document when you are away from your office. Similarly, if you enable iCloud for your contacts, and calendars, if you change details on one device, they will be updated on all of your devices. When Apple first started offering iCloud, there were several issues. It timed out, the syncing was very fussy, and I didn’t use it on my own devices. But for the last few years, I have iCloud enabled on all my devices, so I can access my desktop files on my iPad, all of my photos, contacts and calendars are in sync. Apple is not the only company that offers cloud syncing. If you have a Gmail address, Google also syncs your contacts and calendars. And with Google Drive, you can sync documents and media through Google Photos. Dropbox is another company that allows you to store files in the cloud and access them from all of your devices. They all have a little bit of a different flavor, for example Google is great if you want to work collaboratively with many people through Google docs. Dropbox is great if you have to share big files with colleagues or friends and have a handy cloud back up of your files. And iCloud is a great way to have all your devices in sync. With iCloud, setting up a new machine is much easier. All you have to do is sign in on the new Mac to your iCloud account, and the files just show up in place. Cookie Segelstein is the Macmama, an Apple Certified Service Professional that provides Apple computer consultation and trouble-shooting in your home and office. articles.text: Members of the Piedmont Seniors group are pictured at the Blackhawk Museum in Danville on February 11: (front) Yorkman Lowe (left), Patti Singer, Marianne Gunther-Murphy, Elizabeth Wierzbianska, Merilee Hoffman, Mona Jamieson; (back) Larry Singer, Gregory Jurin, Jim Ayotte, Janet Epstein, Rick Luciano, Susan McCreary, Fred Pemberton, Penny Robb, and Irene Westler. On a lovely, sunny day on February 11, sixteen Piedmont Seniors went on an excursion to the beautiful Blackhawk Museum located on the outskirts of Danville. The museum’s essence is about its founder, Ken Behring, a philanthropist who established “The Wheelchair Foundation”, a nonprofit organization to promote the joy of giving and to deliver a wheelchair to every child, teen and adult who needs one, but cannot afford one. The Seniors arranged for a private docent tour, which greatly enhanced the visit and helped them appreciate the value of the individual collections. The museum, which opened its doors in 1988 as the Behring Auto Museum, has an extensive collection of rare vintage automobiles. The variety of 50 historically significant and artistically inspired automobiles begins from the earliest age of motoring to the contemporary Lamborgini automobile. It is a traveling exhibition, so the automobiles in the museum are constantly changing, making every visit unique. Visitors are given the opportunity to see new, interesting vehicles, as well as some old favorites. Its next exhibit, “The Spirit of the Old West”, is a must for every fourth grader studying California history. There are many Indian artifacts, buffaloes and clothing. This exhibition is dedicated to presenting a balanced narrative of both Native Americans and American settlers and the struggles they all made to survive, from the settlers crossing the plains in a covered wagon, to the Indians being forced from their lands onto reservations. There is an impressive diorama on display, which encompasses most of the back wall of the exhibit space. Here you will see the unique animals that populated the West. Viewers are fortunate that this collection once owned by Jerry Fick was appreciated by Mr. Behring, who saw the value of his collection and purchased what visitors see today. pages.text: Wednesday, February 16, 2022 25 Piedmont Seniors visit Blackhawk Museum Members of the Piedmont Seniors group are pictured at the Blackhawk Museum in Danville on February 11: (front) Yorkman Lowe (left), Patti Singer, Marianne Gunther-Murphy, Elizabeth Wierzbianska, Merilee Hoffman, Mona Jamieson; (back) Larry Singer, Gregory Jurin, Jim Ayotte, Janet Epstein, Rick Luciano, Susan McCreary, Fred Pemberton, Penny Robb, and Irene Westler. On a lovely, sunny day on February 11, sixteen Piedmont Seniors went on an excursion to the beautiful Blackhawk Museum located on the outskirts of Danville. The museum’s essence is about its founder, Ken Behring, a philanthropist who established “The Wheelchair Foundation”, a nonprofit organization to promote the joy of giving and to deliver a wheelchair to every child, teen and adult who needs one, but cannot afford one. The Seniors arranged for a private docent tour, which greatly enhanced the visit and helped them appreciate the value of the individual collections. The museum, which opened its doors in 1988 as the Behring Auto Museum, has an extensive collection of rare vintage automobiles. The variety of 50 historically significant and artistically inspired automobiles begins from the earliest age of motoring to the contemporary Lamborgini automobile. It is a traveling exhibition, so the automobiles in the museum are constantly changing, making every visit unique. Visitors are given the opportunity to see new, interesting vehicles, as well as some old favorites. Its next exhibit, “The Spirit of the Old West”, is a must for every fourth grader studying California history. There are many Indian artifacts, buffaloes and clothing. This exhibition is dedicated to presenting a balanced narrative of both Native Americans and American settlers and the struggles they all made to survive, from the settlers crossing the plains in a covered wagon, to the Indians being forced from their lands onto reservations. There is an impressive diorama on display, which encompasses most of the back wall of the exhibit space. Here you will see the unique animals that populated the West. articles.text: Wednesday Walkers share a group photo on February 9. Pictured are Ken Young, Helen Dong, Albert Chen, Rob Smith, Melba Yee, Quincy Dong, Noemi Alvarado, Jim Kuo, Mike Henn, Jim Kellogg, Wenny Young, Claudia Lopez, Siow Fang Tan, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Priscilla Wanerus, Martin Levy, Brenda Ferrero, Lilly Guardia-Labar, Harriette Louie, Christine Calliste, Pat Keller, Renee Goldhammer, Alan Goldhammer, Elizabeth Richter, Aaron Katzel, Dena Belinkoff, Nancy Henn, John Lenahan, Alicia Rivera, Sarah Johnson, Sherry Jacobs, and Dick Carter. The group was pleased to welcome first time walkers Patti Schneider and Jo Normington with her K-9 best friend Penny Lane. The sun was out again to greet the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group last Wednesday. There was a strong turnout of 34 walkers and one K-9 best friend on the sunny morning. The group had not recently been to Sunnyside Avenue on the south side of Piedmont, and there is some interesting history associated with the buildings nearby on Grand Avenue. Piedmont Historical Society president Gail Lombardi shared some history of this section of Piedmont. In 1929 the Piedmont City Council adopted an ordinance that allowed businesses from the city line to Linda Avenue on the west side of Grand Avenue, and to Fairview Avenue on the east side. Seven months later voters rejected another zoning ordinance to extend the business district to Oakland Avenue. Today, the business district on Grand Avenue remains the same as it was in 1929. The walkers went off in a long line going down Highland Avenue to the corner of Oakland Avenue. When the group reached Latham Street, they regrouped and shared with new walkers Patti Schneider and Jo Normington that Latham is the only “Street” in Piedmont. All other roadways are called Avenue or Drive or Way or something similar. On Oakland Avenue there were early roses and cherry blossoms to enjoy. It took two stoplight cycles for all the walkers cross Grand Avenue before going up to Sunnyside. They stopped at Linda Avenue and learned some more fun history from Gail Lombardi’s research. In 1892 Axel Gruggel built a restaurant on this corner called A Mon Chateau (My Castle). He also had a beer garden in the back on Linda. Over the years, the establishment had different owners, including three bachelors in 1907 who were denied a liquor license when they became available because neighbors didn’t like all of the restaurant’s noise. However, the bachelors continued to sell liquor, and in 1908 they were arrested and their liquor was confiscated. In 1911 a new owner changed the restaurant into “The Piedmont Casino,” where poker was played. But gambling was illegal, and the casino was raided in 1912. Nine card players were arrested and each was fined $55. Not surprisingly, the casino closed soon after. In 1914 the building became the Grand Avenue Grocery Company. It did well until a Piggly Wiggly supermarket opened down the street at Sunnyside. The competition was too much and it closed in 1935. The building was torn down in 1936 and a succession of gas stations occupied the space until 1987 when Chevron sold the property. The current two-story Piedmont Financial Center was built on the site. The walkers found this history interesting but wished the beer garden was still there. The group turned up Sunnyside and climbed to Olive Avenue, where architect and former Piedmont Planning Commissioner Jim Kellogg pointed out a unique home built and owned by contractor Darryl Rush. It has a circular turret ADU and a waving brick front wall that has a built-in seat. The walkers continued up Sunnyside and crossed Oakland Avenue, then through the Linda Avenue Dog Park. When they came out of the park they saw children on the playground across the street at Beach School. The walkers went down Linda Avenue, returning to the site of the A Mon Chateau beer garden (still closed). They went down Grand and crossed it at the stoplight at Wildwood Avenue. The walkers passed the small, triangular park with 15 tall redwood trees; and continued to a short set of stairs that took them to the foot of Warfield Avenue and the “Five Way Stop” intersection. They stayed on Wildwood, going past the Wildwood School. The group came to the Piedmont Park’s lower entrance and took its upper path to the back of the Community Hall where happy preschoolers were playing in their enclosed yard, with a group of high school senior boys having lunch on the steps below them. There was a realization that the walkers’ visit to Sunnyside Avenue had taken them to all three Piedmont elementary schools. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday, rain or shine, at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https:// tinyurl.com/3ethkehu.

In accordance with California Public Contract Code Section 20170, all bids must be presented under sealed cover and include one of the following forms of bidder’s security: cash, cashier’s check made payable to the City, certified check made payable to the City, or a bidder’s bond. The amount of bidder’s security provided must equal at least ten (10) percent of the total of the bid price for the base bid and the additive or deductive items listed in this notice. The successful bidder must submit to the City complete, executed copies of all required documents within ten (10) working days of receiving written notice of award of the project. Bidder’s security of any successful bidder that fails to do so will be forfeited to the City. Such required documents include, but are not limited to, a payment or labor and materials bond in an amount of at least 100 percent of the amount payable by the terms of the project contract and that satisfies the requirements of California Civil Code Section 9554, and a performance bond in an amount of at least 100 percent of the amount payable by the terms of the contract. All project bonds must be executed by an admitted surety insurer in accordance with applicable law and acceptable to the City. In accordance with California Public Contract Code Section 3300, a valid Class A California contractor’s license is required to bid on the project. The City of Piedmont reserves the right to postpone the date and time for the opening of proposals at any time prior to the date and time announced in the advertisement in accordance with applicable law. The City of Piedmont reserves the right to reject any and all bids or to waive any defects or irregularity in bidding in accordance with applicable law. In accordance with California Public Contract Code Section 20103.8, if the City elects to award a contract for performance of the project, the contract will be awarded in accordance with California Public Contract Code Section 20162 and other applicable law to the responsible bidder submitting a responsive bid with the lowest total bid price. All bids will remain valid for 90 days after the bid opening. Except as permitted by law and subject to all applicable remedies, including forfeiture of bidder’s security, bidders may not withdraw their bid during the 90-day period after the bid opening. By order of the City Council of the City of Piedmont, Alameda County, California. Daniel Gonzales February 10, 2022 Public Works Director City of Piedmont 120 Vista Avenue Piedmont, CA 94611

The owner of the residence called the police when the ex-girlfriend of the resident’s son was in the backyard. The resident had previously told Diamond Lopez, a 30-year-old transient, she was not allowed on the property. Police entered the backyard and found her in a wooden structure functioning as a workshop. Through a records search police discovered that she had an outstanding warrant out of San Francisco for narcotics possession. She was also on probation in Alameda County for assault with a deadly weapon, possession of a stolen vehicle, and drunk driving. While attempting to detain the subject, she fled from officers. Officers were eventually able to detain her and placed her in an ambulance for transport to Highland Hospital. When the paramedics slowed at the intersection of Grand and MacArthur Avenue, Lopez jumped out the back of the ambulance. A Piedmont officer was able to detain her and put her back in the ambulance. She was cleared from Highland Hospital at 10:30 p.m. and taken to Santa Rita jail.
